summary: Christ, haloed in gold and seated sideways on a dark donkey, rides with his disciples behind him toward the gate of Jerusalem, while men cut branches from a tree and spread garments in his path and children come out from the city to greet him. Below, four Old Testament prophets in half-length raise their hands toward the scene above, pointing to the fulfilment of their words. It is one of the earliest surviving painted narratives of Palm Sunday.
facts: The Rossano Gospels is a Greek Gospel book written in silver ink on purple-dyed parchment; it was discovered in 1846 in the cathedral of Rossano in Calabria.
Its picture cycle is arranged not in Gospel order but according to the readings of Lent and Holy Week, with prophets below each scene pointing up to the New Testament events they foretold.

notes: Folio numbers follow the conventional numbering of the miniature leaves (1r Lazarus, 1v Entry ... 8v Barabbas); the museum lists the miniatures in this order without folio numbers.

summary: Under the colonnade of the Temple, Christ in a gold mantle turns toward two white-haired priests who question him, while on the right a money-changer sprawls over his overturned table and traders drive out oxen, sheep and a cage of doves. The Greek heading names the episode of those driven out of the Temple. Beneath, prophets hold up their texts in witness.
facts: The diocesan museum's own list of the miniatures calls this scene the 'talk with the priests of the Temple', reflecting the dialogue on the left that accompanies the expulsion on the right.
Like the other picture pages, it combines a single Gospel event with four prophet portraits whose scrolls carry Old Testament verses.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

summary: Christ, as the bridegroom of the parable, stands in a gold mantle before a garden of fruit trees, welcoming the five wise virgins in white who carry lighted torches, while the great golden door is shut against the five foolish virgins in coloured robes on the left. The four rivers of Paradise flow at the bottom of the garden. The parable becomes an image of the Last Judgement and of the kingdom of heaven.
facts: Here Christ himself takes the part of the bridegroom, so that the parable is read directly as a picture of his Second Coming.
The miniature is part of a cycle of 12 scenes from Christ's life and teaching that opens the manuscript.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

summary: On the left Christ reclines at the end of a semicircular table with the apostles crowded around a single dish, one of them — Judas — reaching toward it; on the right Christ stoops to wash Peter's feet in a basin while the other disciples look on. Below, David and other prophets point upward. The two events of the night before the Passion are joined in one strip.
facts: The semicircular couch (sigma) and the reclining posture follow late Roman dining custom, as in other early images of the Last Supper.
The Wikipedia account of the manuscript notes the strange double perspective of this scene, in which the floor seems to tilt up into the table, decorated with birds.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

summary: Christ, haloed and in a brown-gold mantle, stands at the left and places the bread into the hands of a bowing apostle, while the others in white robes approach in a line, their hands covered in reverence. The Greek text above quotes the words of institution, 'he took bread and gave thanks'. The scene presents the Last Supper as a liturgy, with Christ himself as the priest giving communion.
facts: The Communion of the Apostles is spread over two facing pages: here Christ gives the bread, and on the next page the cup.
This is one of the earliest surviving depictions of the Communion of the Apostles, a subject that later became standard in Byzantine church decoration.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

summary: On the facing page Christ, now at the right, offers the cup to an apostle who bends forward to drink, as the remaining disciples wait their turn in a solemn file. The Greek words above recall that he took the cup and gave thanks. Below, prophets raise their hands toward the sacrament.
facts: The diocesan museum describes the Communion of the Apostles as the one scene that occupies two pages of the codex.
The manuscript was restored in 1919 and again in 2012.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

summary: Against a dark hillside under a band of blue night sky, two haloed figures in gold robes bow to the ground in prayer — generally understood as Christ shown twice, kneeling and then fully prostrate, in his agony on the Mount of Olives. The stark composition, almost empty of other detail, conveys the solitude of his prayer before the Passion. Four prophets stand below.
facts: The diocesan museum lists this scene as 'Christ in the Gethsemane', the last of the Passion-week pictures before the canon-table title page.
Showing Christ in successive postures within one frame is a common device of early narrative illumination.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

notes: The reading of the two haloed figures as Christ shown twice is the usual interpretation; the paint surface is worn.

summary: Followed by two disciples, Christ in a gold mantle touches the eyes of the blind man, who then appears again on the right bending over a fountain basin to wash, as onlookers watch. The two moments of the miracle — the anointing and the washing in the pool of Siloam — are told side by side. Prophets below point to the light given to the blind.
facts: Continuous narrative, with the same figure appearing twice in one strip, is used throughout the Rossano miniatures.
The Rossano Gospels contains the Gospel of Matthew and most of Mark; a companion volume with Luke and John is thought to have been lost.

summary: Beside the walled city of Jerusalem, the Good Samaritan — shown with Christ's features, golden halo and gold mantle — bends over the wounded man lying by the road, helped by an angel holding a bowl; then, leading the man on his donkey, he pays the innkeeper. The parable is read as an image of Christ himself coming to heal wounded humanity. Prophets below witness with their scrolls.
facts: Identifying the Samaritan with Christ follows an interpretation of the parable already common among early Church writers.
The angel assisting the Samaritan is not in the Gospel text; it underlines that the helper is divine.

summary: In an apse-like semicircle, Pilate sits enthroned behind a table flanked by imperial standards, surrounded by the crowd who cry out. In the lower register Christ stands calm and haloed among guards, while on the right the bound Barabbas is held by his captors. The page shows the decisive moment of the trial, when the people choose Barabbas over Christ.
facts: Unusually, the Rossano artist did not show the familiar hand-washing of Pilate but the opening of the trial and the choice between Christ and Barabbas, as discussed in the Wikipedia account of the manuscript.
Pilate's commanding position, with Christ lower and to one side, distinguishes these two trial pages from most later versions of the scene.

summary: Beneath large gold uncial letters, Christ stands in a gold mantle between two apostles who hold out loaves and fishes, blessing the food; beside them lie great wicker baskets of bread, and the crowd sits in rows on a green hillside. At each side a haloed prophet leans over a framed panel bearing his prophecy. The miracle is shown as a sign of the Eucharist and of God's abundant care.
facts: Only 44 leaves of this purple Gospel book survive; it was bought at Sinope on the Black Sea in 1899 by a French officer and is now almost entirely in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
Scientific analysis found that the purple of the parchment comes from orchil, a lichen dye, rather than the costly Tyrian purple, and that ultramarine blue was used in the painting.

summary: At the foot of a page of gold lettering, Christ, followed by his disciples, reaches out to touch the eyes of a blind man who stoops toward him, with a second blind man behind, before a cluster of blue-green trees. Two prophets flank the scene, each above a panel inscribed with his text. The unframed figures stand directly on the purple parchment, beneath the Gospel passage they illustrate.
facts: The Sinope miniatures are placed at the foot of the page, directly below the relevant text — a rare early arrangement.
Their style is so close to that of the Rossano Gospels that the two purple manuscripts are usually discussed together and dated to the mid-6th century.

summary: Leaving the walled city on the left, Christ in a gold mantle, accompanied by a disciple in white, stretches out his hand toward a small fig tree, pronouncing that it will bear no more fruit. Two prophets stand above their inscribed panels at either side. The miniature illustrates one of the rarest Gospel subjects in early Christian art.
facts: The manuscript's five miniatures are the Feast of Herod, the Feeding of the Five Thousand, the Feeding of the Four Thousand, the Healing of the Blind of Jericho and the Cursing of the Fig Tree.
The text is written in very large uncials in gold and silver, 15 lines to a page.

summary: Under a gabled canopy framed by columns, Christ sits enthroned and blessing, holding a book, while four monks in dark habits stand around him, two of them presenting a book. The image is generally read as a dedication, the makers of the Gospel offering their work to Christ. Its simple, frontal composition contrasts with the crowded narrative pages that precede it.
facts: The Rabbula Gospels was completed in 586 and signed by the scribe Rabbula, about whom nothing else is known.
Recent scholarship has proposed that its miniatures may come from at least one other manuscript and were bound together with the text of 586 only in the 15th century.
notes: Commons gives fol. 14r; the Wikipedia list places 'Christ with four monks' on the same leaf as the Ascension (fol. 14a). Folio numbering varies between publications.

summary: Beneath a jewelled arch on slender columns, crowned by peacocks, the Virgin stands on a golden footstool holding the Christ Child, who sits upright on her left arm with a halo of his own. The full-length standing Virgin with the Child, shown frontally like an icon, is one of the earliest such images in a manuscript. The peacocks above were an ancient symbol of immortality.
facts: The Wikipedia list of the manuscript's large miniatures places the Theotokos with the infant Jesus on fol. 1b (1v).

After its time in the Middle East — it was at Maipuc in Lebanon in the 11th century and later at Qannubin — the manuscript reached the Laurentian Library in Florence in the late 15th or early 16th century.

summary: A tall arcade framing the Eusebian canon numbers is surrounded by small marginal scenes: at the left John the Baptist lays his hand on the head of Christ standing in the Jordan as the dove descends from a hand-held vessel; at the right the Virgin sits beside the manger where the Child lies, above a scene of the Massacre of the Innocents; enthroned and standing prophets head the margins. The canon tables of the Rabbula Gospels thus become a running picture-Gospel of Christ's life.
facts: The Rabbula Gospels' canon tables, spread over fol. 3v–12v, are framed by arcades with flowers and birds and accompanied by smaller marginal miniatures.
The text is the Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Gospels.

summary: Twelve small panels in a jewelled frame tell the Passion from Palm Sunday onward: Christ rides into Jerusalem to the cry 'Osanna filio David', presides at the Last Supper over a round table with a chalice, prays on the Mount of Olives, washes the disciples' feet beneath a great lampstand, and is betrayed by Judas's kiss; later panels show Peter's sword drawn in the garden, Christ led before his judges, Pilate washing his hands and the cross carried to Golgotha. Brief Latin captions name several scenes. It is the oldest surviving narrative cycle of the Passion in a Latin Gospel book.
facts: The St Augustine Gospels is the oldest surviving illustrated Latin Gospel book; tradition holds that it was brought to England by St Augustine's mission in 597 or sent to him by Pope Gregory the Great in 601.
Only two picture pages survive — this one and the portrait of Luke — giving 24 small scenes from Christ's life, a very rare survival from the old Western Empire.
The manuscript is still used for the oath at the enthronement of each new Archbishop of Canterbury, and in 2023 it was carried in the coronation procession of King Charles III.
notes: Captions were partly added in England in the late 7th or 8th century (per Wikipedia). Identification of each of the lower-row scenes follows the captions where legible.

summary: Saint Luke sits enthroned beneath an arch with his winged ox, and between the columns on either side twelve tiny scenes drawn from his Gospel rise in stacked compartments. In several of them the haloed Christ appears — teaching, in a boat with his disciples, and calling Zacchaeus down from the sycamore tree at the bottom right. The portrait thus presents the evangelist surrounded by the Christ whose story he tells.
facts: When King Charles III was crowned in 2023, the Gospels were carried in the procession open at this very page with the portrait of Luke.
The manuscript once had a portrait and a page of narrative scenes for each evangelist; only those for Luke survive.
notes: The individual identifications of the small side scenes vary between scholars; captions were added later in England.

summary: Christ, alive and open-eyed, stands against the cross with outstretched arms, wrapped in a long robe patterned with interlacing lines; above him two great winged seraphim fill the upper corners, and below at either side stood the lance- and sponge-bearers, now very faint. Though badly worn, the page shows the Insular way of presenting the crucified Christ as triumphant rather than suffering.
facts: Wikipedia describes this page as the oldest Crucifixion in English art; it is one of only two fully decorated pages to survive from the manuscript.
The Durham Gospels was written by the same scribe as the Echternach Gospels and was brought to Durham when the Lindisfarne community fled Viking attacks.
It is used for the oath at the enthronement of each new Bishop of Durham.
notes: The folio is usually cited as fol. 38(3)v because of an irregular foliation.

summary: Christ, with wide-open eyes and a great golden halo, stands before the cross, his body wrapped in a robe of red and purple bands that coil around him like interlace; Stephaton with the sponge and Longinus with the spear kneel close at either side, and two angels sit in the compartments above the cross-arm. The flat, symmetrical design turns the Passion into an icon of Christ's victory.
facts: According to e-codices, the Irish Gospel Book of St Gall was written and illuminated by Irish monks around 750 in Ireland and has 12 decorated pages.
It faces a page showing Christ at the Last Judgement, so that the Crucifixion and Second Coming are seen together at the end of the book.

summary: In the upper register Christ appears in half-length, haloed and frontal, holding a tall cross-staff and an open book, between two angels blowing long trumpets. Below, twelve apostles in two rows look up toward him, each holding a book. It is a concise Insular image of the Second Coming, facing the Crucifixion on the opposite page.
facts: The manuscript's twelve decorated pages include evangelist portraits, a carpet page and this closing pair of Crucifixion and Last Judgement.
Images are provided by e-codices, the Virtual Manuscript Library of Switzerland, under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.
notes: Image from e-codices (not Commons); licence CC BY-NC 4.0 per the e-codices IIIF manifest.

summary: The opening letter T of the prayer 'Te igitur' at the start of the Canon of the Mass is formed by the cross itself, on which Christ hangs with open eyes and a cross-nimbus, blood streaming from his side, beneath the inscription IHS XPS; two winged angels swoop toward him from above the cross-arm. It is among the earliest images of the Crucifixion placed at the heart of the eucharistic prayer, a practice that became standard in later missals.
facts: Wikipedia describes this page as perhaps the oldest image of the Crucifixion in a Frankish manuscript; the verso of folio 1 shows the Virgin Mary holding a cross and a censer.

The book was at Cambrai Cathedral under Bishop Hildoard (c. 790–800), was later given by William of Gellone to his abbey of Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, passed to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 1638 and entered the French national library in 1796.
notes: Place of origin is debated (Meaux, Cambrai or another northern French centre).

summary: Beneath a stylised arch topped by two beasts' heads, Christ stands frontally with arms outstretched, a large, calm figure with curling hair and beard, while two much smaller men seize him by the arms. The arch encloses the words 'Et hymno dicto exierunt in montem Oliveti' — 'when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives'. Christ's open, cross-like pose anticipates the Crucifixion.
facts: The scholar Françoise Henry attributed this page and the Temptation to the artist she called 'the Illustrator'.
Its verso carries a fully decorated text page with Christ's words 'Tunc dicit illis Iesus omnes vos scandalum' (Matthew 26:31).
notes: The Commons file description says '114v' but the miniature is on fol. 114r (Wikipedia; Trinity College).

summary: Christ appears from the waist up on the pinnacle of the Temple, drawn as a great patterned roof, holding a scroll; at his left a small black, winged figure of Satan tempts him, while two angels hover above. A crowd of heads fills the left side, and within the Temple a small half-figure appears in a doorway, with more people gathered below. It illustrates the moment in Luke when the devil sets Christ on the pinnacle of the Temple.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the crowd to Christ's right may represent his disciples; the figure in the Temple doorway has been variously interpreted.
The facing page (fol. 203r) begins 'Iesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto' (Luke 4:1), the opening of the Temptation narrative, in a fully decorated text page.

summary: In the margin beside the text of Psalm 46, Christ sits enthroned and blessing within an oval mandorla carried up by four angels; below, on a hilltop among olive trees, the Virgin stands in a dark mantle among the apostles, who gaze and gesture upward. The image interprets the psalm verse 'God is gone up with a shout' as a prophecy of Christ's Ascension.
facts: The Khludov Psalter is a 'marginal psalter': the outer edges of its pages were left blank to be filled with pictures, linked to particular verses by small arrows.
It is one of only three illuminated Byzantine psalters to survive from the 9th century, a generation after the end of Iconoclasm.
notes: Folio not recorded on the Commons file (photographed from a reprint). The psalm number ΜΖ (46, Septuagint numbering) is visible beside the miniature.

summary: On this damaged frontispiece, David the psalmist sits beneath a broad arch on a column, while above him, set within the arch, a large medallion contains the bust of Christ. Small figures stand at either side. Placing Christ above David at the opening of the Psalter presents the psalms as words that look forward to him.
facts: The Russian Orthodox Encyclopedia, the source of the image, identifies it as folio 1v of the manuscript.
The Psalter was kept on Mount Athos until 1847, when it was taken to Moscow; it later belonged to the merchant Aleksey Khludov, whose name it bears.

summary: The saintly Patriarch Nikephoros, in white vestments, holds up a round icon with the bust of Christ and tramples the iconoclast John the Grammarian, who lies on the ground among scattered coins; above, Saint Peter treads on Simon Magus. The image of Christ held aloft is the point of the whole page: the defence of icons as a confession of the Incarnation.
facts: Many of the Khludov miniatures are polemics against the Iconoclasts, with John the Grammarian caricatured by wild, bristling hair.
Explanatory captions are written beside the figures; here they name the patriarch Nikephoros and his defeated opponent.
notes: Christ appears here as a painted icon held by the patriarch. The psalm number ΝΒ (51) is visible. Folio not recorded on the Commons file.

summary: In the margin at the left, the patriarch Nikephoros stands holding an icon of Christ, while at the foot of the page an iconoclast assembly sits around an enthroned ruler and one figure reaches toward a medallion icon of Christ beside a vessel of whitewash. The page contrasts reverence for Christ's image with its destruction, illustrating the psalm's rejection of 'the assembly of evildoers'.
facts: The Commons description identifies the scene as the iconoclast council of 815 under Emperor Leo V, with Patriarch Theodotos, and the icon being destroyed by John the Grammarian and Antony of Syllaion.
According to Wikipedia, some scholars attribute the psalter to the Stoudios monastery, others to imperial workshops soon after the restoration of icons in 843.
notes: Identification of the figures follows the Commons description; the lower scene is badly worn. Psalm number and folio not verified.

summary: At the top of a steep red mountain, Christ stands in a blue mandorla between Moses and Elijah, while on the slopes below the three apostles fall to the ground, dazzled by the light. The tall, narrow composition fits the margin of the page beside the psalm text it illuminates.
facts: Byzantine marginal psalters commonly attached the Transfiguration to the verse 'Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name' (Psalm 88:13 in the Septuagint).
The Khludov Psalter contains 169 folios and measures about 195 by 150 mm.
notes: The specific psalm verse beside this miniature is not legible in the low-resolution image; the Tabor association is the usual one in this tradition.

summary: The book opens with a full-page image of Christ seated frontally on a lyre-backed throne with a cushion, a great cross-nimbus behind his head; he blesses with his right hand and holds an open Gospel book on his knee. Much of the paint has flaked away, revealing the underdrawing of his robes, but the majestic, iconic figure remains clear. Placed before the imperial portraits, it presents Christ as the true ruler from whom earthly authority descends.
facts: The frontispiece Christ is followed by portraits of the Empress Eudokia with her sons and of Emperor Basil I, so that the imperial family appears under Christ's authority.

The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
notes: Fol. Av is the first of the prefatory leaves (lettered A–C) before the homilies.

summary: Three registers tell the climax of Christ's Passion and its triumph: at the top Christ hangs on the cross between the two thieves with the Virgin and John and the soldiers; in the middle his body is taken down and laid in the tomb; at the bottom the risen Christ greets the holy women with 'Chairete' ('Rejoice'), beside the empty sepulchre. The page faces Gregory's homily on Easter.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
The inscription ΧΑΙΡΕΤΕ, Christ's greeting to the women in Matthew's Gospel, is written above the risen Christ in the lowest register.
notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio.

summary: Within a golden medallion at the top of the page Christ sits enthroned and blessing, while six-winged seraphim and ranks of angels holding staffs fill the sky beneath him; at the left the prophet Isaiah, labelled, reels back in awe. The inscription names the scene as the vision of Isaiah, in which the Lord appears 'sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up'. Byzantine artists showed the Lord of the vision with the features of Christ.
facts: The heading at the top left reads 'Vision of Isaiah' (ΟΡΑΣΙΣ ΗΣΑΙΟΥ).
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.

summary: Christ stands in a pale mandorla on the summit of Mount Tabor between Elijah and Moses, his garments shining; below, Peter, James and John fall back on the rocky slope, shielding their eyes. The single full-page composition, with its gold-haloed figures against a blue ground, is one of the best preserved in the manuscript.

summary: The top register, headed 'the calling of the apostles', shows Christ summoning Peter and Andrew and the sons of Zebedee from their boats, calling Zacchaeus down from the sycamore tree, and calling Matthew from his table heaped with coins. The next register shows Christ with the rich young man and calling Nathanael beneath the fig tree; healings follow below. In every scene Christ, haloed and in a purple mantle, takes the initiative of the call.

summary: The top register shows the prophet Nathan rebuking the kneeling King David; the middle tells the parable of the man who fell among thieves on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, with the haloed Christ, wearing a cross-nimbus, coming to his aid; in the lowest register Christ, followed by his disciples, approaches a bier where a dead woman lies surrounded by mourners. The page sets repentance and Christ's mercy side by side.

Captions in Greek name the places Jerusalem and Jericho in the parable scene.

summary: At the top the boy Christ sits enthroned behind a table in the Temple between seated teachers, while Joseph and Mary arrive at the left; at the right the adult Christ stands apart. The middle register shows Christ performing healings beside a tall building, and at the bottom he stands between two apostles blessing the loaves as baskets of bread are filled and the crowd sits on the grass.

summary: In the top register Christ heals a leper covered in spots and a man stripped to the waist, and frees a raging demoniac by the tombs; in the middle he meets a centurion with soldiers before a building and raises Peter's mother-in-law from her bed; at the bottom he stands on the sea and stretches out his hand to the sinking Peter while the apostles watch from the boat. The page gathers Christ's miracles of healing and rescue.

summary: In the upper register Christ calls Lazarus, still wrapped in his grave-clothes, from the tomb while Mary and Martha kneel; beside it Christ reclines at table as a woman anoints his feet. Below, Christ rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, followed by the apostles, as children and townspeople come out of the city gate to greet him.

The framed, almost icon-like page is one of the most elaborate in the manuscript.

summary: In the upper register, labelled in Greek, Christ anoints the eyes of the man born blind, who then bends to wash in the pool of Siloam while an angel hovers above; to the right Christ watches as the poor widow drops her two small coins into the tall temple treasury. Below, friends let a paralysed man down through a roof to Christ, who sits among the crowd. The page joins Christ's healing power to his praise of humble generosity.
facts: The Greek captions read 'Christ healing the man blind from birth', 'the pool of Siloam' and 'the widow with the two mites'.

summary: Christ, beardless and youthful with a golden cross-nimbus, sits frontally on a cushioned throne against a deep blue disc, blessing and holding a jewelled book. Around him a broad ring holds medallions of the four evangelist symbols and small busts of prophets, while gold capitals above and below declare that the four living creatures proclaim the sacred gifts of Christ. It is the central image of one of the most sumptuous books made for Charlemagne's court.
facts: The Lorsch Gospels is now divided: Matthew, Mark and the prefatory pages are in Alba Iulia, Romania, Luke and John in the Vatican Library, and the ivory covers in the Vatican Museums and the Victoria and Albert Museum.

It was recorded in Lorsch Abbey's library catalogue of 830 as a Gospel book 'written in gold ... with ivory tablets'; in 1622, during the Thirty Years' War, it was taken from Heidelberg and broken in two to make it easier to sell.
The German Wikipedia notes that its Majestas Domini influenced later Ottonian painting, for example the Majestas of the Gero Codex.

summary: Above the arcade framing the gold-lettered preface to Matthew's Gospel, a lunette is filled with crowds of figures arranged in tiers, with framed busts among them; at the very top, in a blue medallion, Christ sits enthroned. The composition visualises Matthew's genealogy, with the generations of Christ's ancestors leading up to him.
facts: The Lorsch Gospels takes its name from Lorsch Abbey, for which it was probably made; it is also called the Codex Aureus because it is written entirely in gold ink.
According to German Wikipedia, the book contained four evangelist portraits and a Majestas Domini, twelve canon tables and prefaces to each Gospel.
notes: Folio not given by the Commons source. Identification of the tiers of figures as Christ's ancestors follows the Matthew prologue (Argumentum) that the page introduces.

The page is a classic Tours image of the Majestas Domini.
facts: The Gospels of Lothair was made for Emperor Lothair I at Saint-Martin de Tours in 849–851; it has 221 leaves written in gold ink and six miniatures.
Its production was overseen by one Sigilaus, and it contains the earliest depiction of Lothair, possibly the earliest monarch portrait in a biblical manuscript.

summary: At the top of a monumental architectural frontispiece, the Lamb of God stands in a medallion against the heavens while the twenty-four elders, in two groups, rise from their seats and raise their crowns toward him. Christ is shown here in the symbolic form of the Apocalypse, the Lamb who was slain.
facts: The manuscript was given to the abbey of Saint-Médard at Soissons by Louis the Pious and his wife Judith in 827 and remained there until the French Revolution.
It belongs to the Court or 'Ada' School of Charlemagne; besides twelve decorated canon tables it has six full-page miniatures, including a Fountain of Life modelled on the Godescalc Evangelistary.

summary: Within the round initial O of the Palm Sunday prayers, Christ hangs dead on the cross, his head bowed; a female figure, Ecclesia, holds up a chalice to catch the blood and water from his side, while the Virgin and John stand at either side, a serpent coils at the foot of the cross and the Sun and Moon look on from above. facts: Wikipedia notes that this Crucifixion is of a new type, the dead 'Christus patiens' rather than the triumphant living Christ that had been the norm.

facts: The Vivian Bible was commissioned by Count Vivian, lay abbot of Saint-Martin de Tours, in 845 and presented to Charles the Bald in 846, as shown in its presentation miniature; it has 423 leaves measuring 495 by 345 mm.

facts: The Moutier-Grandval Bible is a one-volume Bible of the whole Vulgate as revised by Alcuin of York, and one of three surviving illustrated Bibles made at Tours (British Library description on Commons).
Its four full-page miniatures — Genesis, Exodus, the Majestas Domini and the Apocalypse — form one of the classic Carolingian Bible cycles.

facts: The Codex Aureus of St Emmeram was produced for Charles the Bald in 870; its jewelled gold cover is among the very few treasure bindings of that date to survive.
Charles gave the book to Arnulf of Carinthia, who donated it to St Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg, where it remained for most of its history.

facts: Only an unfinished fragment of ten leaves survives, but it has two initial pages and five full-page miniatures; it entered the royal library in Paris in 1732 from the estate of Jean-Baptiste Colbert.
The manuscript is attributed to the court school of Charles the Bald, whose location after the destruction of Saint-Martin at Tours in 853 is disputed.

facts: Made between 984 and 991 for the private use of the young King Otto III, this is the only surviving prayer book of an Ottonian king; it is tiny (15 × 12 cm), written in gold on painted purple, with five full-page miniatures.
German Wikipedia describes this as the first miniature, facing a Deesis on the recto.

facts: The Gero Codex was probably produced at Reichenau between 950 and 970 and is one of the first and most splendid works of the 'Eburnant group' of early Ottonian manuscripts.
Its Christ in Majesty is copied from a Carolingian model, the Lorsch Gospels, and was in turn borrowed by the Petershausen Sacramentary.

summary: Within a medallion framed by a gold scale pattern, Christ sits frontally on a cushioned throne against a blue ground, blessing and holding an open book on his knee. facts: German Wikipedia notes that the double page of the enthroned Ecclesia and the enthroned Christ, like the Majestas of the Gero Codex, derives from the Lorsch Gospels.
The sacramentary was made around 980 at Reichenau for solemn services, probably by the scribe Anno of the Gero Codex, and reached the abbey of Petershausen only later, probably after a fire of 1159.

The British Library describes this page as the preface to the blessing for Palm Sunday.

summary: Inside a great gold initial O, a figure with a cross-nimbus sits enthroned on a rainbow, blessing with the right hand and holding a book, his green mantle falling in swirling folds. facts: The Benedictional of St Æthelwold, written by the monk Godeman for Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester (963–984), is regarded as the masterpiece of late Anglo-Saxon illumination; it has 28 full-page miniatures.
The Latin inscription declares the Trinity to be one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the blessing is that for Trinity Sunday.
notes: The figure personifies the Triune God; it is given Christ's cross-nimbus, as was customary, but the image is a Trinity rather than a narrative depiction of Christ.

summary: In delicate tinted line drawing, Christ hangs dead on the cross, his head sunk on his shoulder, beneath the inscription 'Hic est Nazarenus rex Iudeorum'; the Virgin, at left, raises her veil to her weeping face, and John, at right, writes on a scroll while gazing up at him. The fluttering drapery and fine, nervous line make this one of the most moving images in Anglo-Saxon art.
facts: Wikipedia notes that this coloured outline drawing draws on the style of the Utrecht Psalter, which was then in England.
The same artist seems to have worked at Fleury Abbey and at Saint-Bertin, Saint-Omer, where he contributed to the Boulogne Gospels.
The psalter's script inspired the 'foundational hand' of the 20th-century calligrapher Edward Johnston.

summary: In the upper part of a page framed with acanthus, Christ sits in a mandorla held aloft by four angels, holding a book; below, King Edgar, between the Virgin Mary and St Peter — patrons of the New Minster — raises the charter up toward him. facts: The New Minster Charter commemorates Edgar's conversion of the New Minster, Winchester, into a Benedictine monastery in 966; every page is written in gold, which was unusual in England.
This frontispiece is the charter's only fully illuminated page and is among the earliest works of the Winchester School.

facts: The two leaves with the so-called 'Final Four Miniatures', dating to the late 6th or early 7th century, were bound into this Gospel book of 989.
The book of 989 was made at the monastery of Bgheno-Noravank in Syunik for Bishop Stepanos; its covers are two carved ivory plaques, probably Byzantine work of the 6th century.

facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.
